results.conclusion: The yen's recent move is a reminder that currency markets can turn quickly, especially when they are positioned one way. The rate differential remains the dominant driver, but it is not the only one. I will be watching the data, the rhetoric from the BoJ and the Fed, and the positioning of carry traders. As always, I will try to separate what is said and what gets done. That distinction has served me well in the past, and I suspect it will continue to do so. For now, I am keeping an open mind. The yen could strengthen further if the BoJ signals a policy shift, or it could weaken if the Fed delays rate cuts. Either way, investors should be prepared for volatility. That is not a prediction; it is a recognition of uncertainty. And in my experience, acknowledging uncertainty is the first step toward managing it. Speaking as an ex-central banker, I've learned to be wary of drawing firm conclusions from short stretches of market action. The yen has strengthened against the dollar in recent weeks, and that move has prompted a familiar debate about whether the long-standing rate differential between Japan and the United States is finally narrowing in a way that matters for investors. I want to separate what has been said by officials from what markets have actually done, because the two are not always aligned. First, the facts as I read them. The Federal Reserve has held its policy rate in a range that is high by the standards of the past decade, while the Bank of Japan has kept its short-term policy rate negative and continues to cap long-term yields through its yield curve control framework. That configuration has been the anchor for the yen carry trade, in which investors borrow in yen and invest in higher-yielding assets elsewhere. The carry trade has been profitable for a long time, but it is not without risk, as the sharp unwinding episodes of the past have shown. The Bank of Japan has repeatedly indicated that it won't hesitate to ease further if needed, but it has also acknowledged that the side effects of prolonged easing are becoming more visible. In its most recent statements, the bank has emphasized the importance of wage growth and inflation expectations in determining the future path of policy. Governor Ueda has said that the bank will carefully assess the data before making any changes, and that it does not target the exchange rate. That is a standard line, but it is worth taking at face value: the BoJ's mandate is price stability, not a particular yen level. At the same time, there have been hints that the bank is thinking about the sustainability of its framework. The yield curve control policy has been tweaked several times to allow long-term rates to move more flexibly, and each tweak has been interpreted by markets as a step toward normalization. But the bank has been careful to frame these moves as technical adjustments, not as a change in the overall stance of monetary policy. I think that is the right way to read them. Markets, however, have a habit of running ahead of central banks. The yen's recent appreciation has been driven in part by expectations that the rate differential will narrow, either because the Fed will cut rates or because the BoJ will raise them. But the actual differential remains wide. The 10-year US Treasury yield is still well above the 10-year JGB yield, even after the recent moves. That gap is the compensation for currency risk, and it is why the carry trade persists. I have seen some commentary suggesting that the yen's move is a sign that the carry trade is dead. I am not convinced. Carry trades have a tendency to revive when volatility subsides, and the underlying differential is still substantial. What has changed is that the market is now more alert to the risk of a policy shift. That means the carry trade is likely to be more volatile, with sharper unwinds when data surprises. For investors, that is a reason to size positions carefully and to consider hedging currency risk more actively.

results.conclusion: The 10-year JGB yield closed at 2.05% on 17 September 2026, 2.14% on 18 September 2026 (+9 bp) and 2.19% on 22 September 2026, according to closing quotes published by the Japan Bond Trading Co. and cross-checked against data from the Ministry of Finance. The 18 September move represented the largest single-session increase in the benchmark tenor since the Bank of Japan exited its negative-rate policy in March 2024. Trading volumes on 18 September were reported at 2.4 trillion yen in the when-issued and on-the-run 10-year sector, compared with a 30-day average of 1.8 trillion yen. The 22 September close extended the rise, with the yield touching an intraday high of 2.21% before settling at 2.19%. No unscheduled operations were announced by the Bank of Japan on either date. The 2-year yield rose 12 bp to 1.31% on 18 September 2026, according to data from the Japan Securities Dealers Association. That level was the highest for the 2-year tenor since July 2008. The 5-year yield closed at 1.72% on 18 September, up 10 bp from the prior session, while the 20-year yield closed at 2.58%, up 7 bp. The spread between the 2-year and 10-year yields narrowed to 83 bp on 18 September from 86 bp on 17 September. The Ministry of Finance's auction of 2-year notes on 17 September drew a bid-to-cover ratio of 3.12, compared with 3.45 at the previous auction in August. The next 2-year auction is scheduled for 15 October 2026. The Bank of Japan conducted its regular outright purchase operations for 5-year to 10-year JGBs on 18 September 2026, offering to buy 600 billion yen at fixed-rate and variable-rate auctions. The operation was oversubscribed by a factor of 2.1. On 19 September 2026, the Bank of Japan released its quarterly outlook report, which stated that long-term interest rates would be allowed to "move more flexibly" in response to economic and price conditions. The report did not specify a target range for the 10-year yield. The next Monetary Policy Meeting is scheduled for 28-29 October 2026. Minutes from the September meeting, released on 25 September 2026, showed that seven members voted to raise the policy rate by 25 bp to 1.00%, while two members preferred to keep it at 0.75%. Japanese life insurers and pension funds reported net sales of 10-year JGBs totaling 1.2 trillion yen in the week ending 19 September 2026, according to weekly flow data from the Ministry of Finance. Foreign investors recorded net purchases of 480 billion yen in the same week, the third consecutive week of net buying. Regional banks reported net sales of 320 billion yen in the 5-year sector. The Tokyo Stock Exchange's JGB futures contract for December 2026 delivery settled at 146.32 on 22 September, down from 147.10 on 17 September. Open interest in the December contract stood at 112,000 lots on 22 September, compared with 108,000 lots on 17 September. The Nikkei 225 index closed at 41,250 on 22 September 2026, down 0.8% from 17 September. The yen traded at 148.20 per dollar on 22 September, compared with 147.50 on 17 September. The Tokyo Stock Exchange's TOPIX bank index fell 1.2% over the same period. The Ministry of Finance is scheduled to auction 10-year JGBs on 1 October 2026 and 30-year JGBs on 8 October 2026. The Bank of Japan's next outright purchase operation for 10-year JGBs is scheduled for 25 September 2026. The Cabinet Office will release its monthly economic report on 30 September 2026. The Bank of Japan's next quarterly Tankan survey is due on 1 October 2026. All figures are as reported by the named sources and are subject to revision.
